evidence_records.Full citation: De Paoli, Stefano, and Walter Stan Mathis. 2025. Codebook Reduction and Saturation: Novel Observations on Inductive Thematic Saturation for Large Language Models and Initial Coding in Thematic Analysis. arXiv:2503.04859v1.
evidence_records.Title: Codebook Reduction and Saturation: Novel observations on Inductive Thematic Saturation for Large Language Models and initial coding in Thematic Analysis
evidence_records.Authors: Stefano De Paoli; Walter Stan Mathis
evidence_records.Publication history notes: arXiv v1; manuscript explicitly labels itself a draft that may contain errors
evidence_records.Citation count, source, and retrieval da: not collected; official arXiv full text inspected 2026-08-24
evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: De Paoli–Mathis inductive thematic saturation series
evidence_records.Research objective: Characterize run/order variability in LLM initial coding and compare a zero-shot duplicate-reduction prompt with a DSPy-compiled reducer for an inductive thematic saturation ratio.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: inductive thematic analysis and inductive thematic saturation
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: GPT-3.5-Turbo-16k independently generates up to 15 code-description-quote triples per interview; a second LLM stage reduces duplicates either with a zero-shot prompt or a DSPy ChainOfThought prompt compiled from labeled code pairs; unique/total code ratio is treated as ITS and compared across repeated runs and interview sequences.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: inductive initial coding followed by learned/few-shot semantic duplicate classification
evidence_records.Dataset name: UK NHS trial-transparency interview dataset from De Vito et al. (2023)
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: source interview dataset cited with UK Data Service DOI; exact reuse package for this experiment not separately deposited
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: 7 repetitions of one 12-interview sequence plus 6 alternative sequences; 162–187 initial codes per run/sequence
evidence_records.Document length: full interview passed one at a time; lengths not reported
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: health-services professional interviews; secondary data, sensitivity handling not reported
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: temperature 0; zero-shot initial-coding Prompt_1; zero-shot duplicate reducer Prompt_2; DSPy ChainOfThought/RandomSearch compiled reducer using demonstrations
evidence_records.Fine-tuning or adaptation: DSPy prompt compilation from 198 code-pair examples (99 different and 99 synthetic similar pairs manually adjusted), drawn from four open datasets with an 80/20 split; no weight fine-tuning
evidence_records.Agent roles: initial coder and pairwise duplicate judge/codebook reducer
evidence_records.Human role: authors design prompts, construct and manually adjust training pairs, select the ITS formulation, and interpret semantic-similarity matrices; no independent human validation of final codebooks
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: interview for initial coding; code-description pair for duplicate reduction
evidence_records.Generated outputs: initial codes with descriptions and quotations, reduced cumulative unique codebooks, ITS ratios and semantic-similarity matrices
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: initial codes retain representative quotations, but reduced-code provenance and source-level traceability are not fully evaluated
evidence_records.Baselines: zero-shot Prompt_2 reducer versus DSPy-compiled reducer; repeated same-sequence and alternative-sequence analyses
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: 7 repetitions of sequence 1 plus 6 interview sequences; random seeds not reported
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: unique/total code ITS ratio, range, coefficient of variation, linear fits and all-MiniLM-L6-v2 cosine-similarity matrices
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: none reported for code validity, duplicate decisions, or thematic adequacy
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: authors only; independent evaluators not reported
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: descriptive ranges and coefficients of variation; illustrative linear regression and semantic-similarity matrices
evidence_records.Principal results: Initial-code totals varied from 162 to 182 across repeated runs despite temperature 0. DSPy-reduced ITS was more stable than Prompt_2 (CoV 3.88% versus 23.34% across repeated runs; 2.79% versus 19.4% across sequences), yielding roughly 65–81 unique codes and ITS about .40–.43.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: DSPy described as more complex, technically demanding and potentially more expensive; no measured time or cost
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: not reported for this secondary analysis
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: verbatim core prompts and the compiled DSPy prompt are included in the appendix; source dataset DOI cited; executable code and full outputs not reported
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: draft status; DSPy complexity/cost and programming skill; training examples were partly synthetic and manually adjusted; different training datasets may change results
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: ITS is a duplicate-rate statistic, not evidence of interpretive validity or theoretical/data saturation. The DSPy validation metric reportedly returned True on every training example, and no independent human judgment establishes that pair reductions or final codebooks are substantively correct.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Direct extension of De Paoli and Mathis (2024), arXiv:2411.12142, using the same ITS concept and authors' earlier LLM thematic-analysis procedures.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Supports explicit run-stability and codebook-reduction checks, but argues against using a stable ITS ratio as a stand-alone quality criterion without human semantic validation.

evidence_records.Full citation: Simon, Sebastian, Sreecharan Sankaranarayanan, Elham Tajik, Conrad Borchers, Bahar Shahrokhian, Francesco Balzan, Sebastian Strauß, Sree Aurovindh Viswanathan, Amine Hatun Ataş, Mia Čarapina, Li Liang, and Berkan Celik. 2025. Comparing a Human’s and a Multi-Agent System’s Thematic Analysis: Assessing Qualitative Coding Consistency. Lecture Notes in Computer Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-98420-4_5. Preprint: https://doi.org/10.35542/osf.io/ez8wc_v1.
evidence_records.Title: Comparing a Human’s and a Multi-Agent System’s Thematic Analysis: Assessing Qualitative Coding Consistency
evidence_records.Authors: Sebastian Simon; Sreecharan Sankaranarayanan; Elham Tajik; Conrad Borchers; Bahar Shahrokhian; Francesco Balzan; Sebastian Strauß; Sree Aurovindh Viswanathan; Amine Hatun Ataş; Mia Čarapina; Li Liang; Berkan Celik
evidence_records.Publication type: published conference/book chapter with OSF preprint
evidence_records.Peer-reviewed status: published Springer LNCS chapter; exact peer-review procedure not independently verified
evidence_records.Publication history notes: Inspected artifact labels itself PREPRINT and has OSF DOI 10.35542/osf.io/ez8wc_v1; Crossref also records the same title/authors as Springer LNCS chapter DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-98420-4_5
evidence_records.Citation count, source, and retrieval da: Crossref local export recorded 1 citation; inspected OSF full text 2026-08-24
evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: Simon et al. CSCL survey/manual-iTA/MAS evaluation family
evidence_records.Research objective: Define benchmark and expert-review criteria for automated inductive thematic analysis and compare a Claude 3.5 Sonnet multi-agent analysis with a prior four-expert human analysis.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: end-to-end inductive thematic analysis following Braun and Clarke
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: Amazon Bedrock custom orchestration decomposes an iTA process description into three independent coding agents, a consensus agent, and an automatically added translator when needed; outputs are compared response-by-response and theme-by-theme with the prior human analysis in a blinded external-expert template.
evidence_records.Domain: artificial intelligence in education / computer-supported collaborative learning
evidence_records.Dataset name: CSCL scholars' definitions survey (Simon et al. prior work)
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: anonymous survey data and process prompt available on OSF
evidence_records.Number of documents: 184 substantive responses to four open-ended survey questions; 10 minimal responses excluded
evidence_records.Number of participants: survey respondent count is not clearly reconciled with response count in the inspected manuscript
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: 184 analyzed responses; AI averaged 1.7 codes per response versus 2.5 for humans; about 5 AI themes versus 9.5 human themes per question
evidence_records.Language: primarily English with some French responses automatically translated
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: survey consent covered full anonymous publication and reuse
evidence_records.Exact model/version: Claude 3.5 Sonnet via Amazon Bedrock; snapshot identifier and inference parameters not reported
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: high-level agentic process prompt; orchestrator task decomposition; three parallel coding calls followed by consensus/reconciliation and optional translation
evidence_records.Agent roles: orchestrator, three independent coding agents, consensus/reconciliation agent, and dynamically added translator
evidence_records.Human role: four domain experts produced the reference analysis; two external CSCL experts independently reviewed shuffled human/AI codes and themes; authors designed the benchmark rubric
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: individual survey response for codes; complete per-question code/thematic structures for themes
evidence_records.Generated outputs: codes, consensus codebook, themes, descriptions and final analysis narrative
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: each response is paired with its human and AI code sets in the evaluation; themes list their constituent codes; full narrative provenance is weaker
evidence_records.Baselines: prior four-expert manual iTA of the same corpus
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: one reported MAS analysis; seeds and repeat runs not reported
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: descriptive proportions, average codes/themes and exact binomial tests for authorship identification
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: two independent external PhD experts reviewed shuffled code sets for correctness, comparative preference and perceived source, then themes for clarity, representativeness, relevance, relatedness and source
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: four CSCL experts in the manual benchmark; two external PhD experts in CSCL with more than five years' experience
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: manual benchmark Krippendorff's alpha=.934; no inter-rater coefficient reported for the two external evaluators, whose judgments diverged substantially
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: descriptive percentages and exact binomial tests for selected authorship-identification results
evidence_records.Principal results: AI codes were individually judged appropriate in 91% of cases versus 81% for human codes, but evaluator 1 preferred human code sets for questions 1/2/4 (87%/71%/56%) while evaluator 2 usually judged both good (90%/92%/88%). Experts jointly found only 3 of 22 proposed related-theme pairs; the AI final report lacked a comprehensive narrative.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: automation and translation described as reducing tedious work; no measured time or API cost
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: prior survey obtained consent for anonymous publication/reuse; model-provider privacy, IRB and data-transfer controls not reported
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: OSF dataset and high-level process prompt link reported; preprint DOI available; system code, exact model snapshot, parameters and complete run logs not reported
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: single domain-specific dataset; need broader tests; parameters and agent prompts could be optimized
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: Only two external evaluators produced sharply different comparative judgments, yet no reliability statistic is reported. The manuscript also refers to 184 analyzed responses but elsewhere bases a binomial framing on 200, and indistinguishability is not evidence of interpretive equivalence.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Uses the same CSCL corpus and prior manual analysis as Simon et al.; uses the authors' earlier Claude 3.5 Sonnet MAS architecture, making it a dependent evaluation rather than an independent replication.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Strongly motivates blinded, code- and theme-level human evaluation plus narrative-quality assessment; the evaluator divergence and absent reruns argue for more reviewers and explicit plurality handling.

evidence_records.Full citation: Moskalewicz, Marcin, Anna Sterna, Karolina Drożdż, Kacper Dudzic, Marek Pokropski, and Paula Flores. 2026. Computational Phenomenology of Borderline Personality Disorder: A Comparative Evaluation of LLM-Simulated Expert Personas and Human Clinical Experts. ETHICAIA’26 Workshop on Ethics in Clinical AI Applications at IJCAI-ECAI 2026. arXiv:2508.19008v3.
evidence_records.Title: Computational Phenomenology of Borderline Personality Disorder: A Comparative Evaluation of LLM-Simulated Expert Personas and Human Clinical Experts
evidence_records.Authors: Marcin Moskalewicz; Anna Sterna; Karolina Drożdż; Kacper Dudzic; Marek Pokropski; Paula Flores
evidence_records.Venue: ETHICAIA’26 Workshop on Ethics in Clinical AI Applications at IJCAI-ECAI 2026
evidence_records.Peer-reviewed status: workshop acceptance shown in manuscript; archival peer-review status not verified
evidence_records.Publication history notes: Database record was arXiv:2508.19008v3 and dated 2025, but the inspected current full text identifies ETHICAIA’26 at IJCAI-ECAI 2026, carries 2026 copyright, and should be treated as a 2026 version family
evidence_records.Citation count, source, and retrieval da: not collected; official arXiv v3 full text inspected 2026-08-24
evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: Sterna/Moskalewicz human phenomenology reference study plus 2026 LLM comparative reanalysis
evidence_records.Research objective: Test whether persona-prompted frontier LLMs can reproduce, complement or challenge a human phenomenological thematic analysis of clinical life-story interviews.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: phenomenologically informed inductive thematic analysis / computational phenomenology
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Pro and Claude 4 Opus each perform three persona-prompted thematic analyses and synthesize them; internal experts map overlap and verify omitted themes against raw data, two blinded external experts rate human/model outputs on eight validity dimensions, embeddings compare semantics/style, and 115 lay raters assess isolated theme titles/descriptions.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: hybrid: inductive analysis constrained by a named investigator persona, prior meta-synthesis, textbook method, demographics and research questions
evidence_records.Dataset name: 24 Polish inpatient BPD life-story interviews from the authors' prior reference study
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: raw clinical transcripts not reported as public; prompts and derived outputs included in appendices/supplement
evidence_records.Number of participants: 24 clinical interview participants plus 4 expert judges and 115 Prolific public evaluators
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: more than 150,000 words; 12 human themes, 5 GPT themes, 7 Gemini themes and 11 Claude themes
evidence_records.Language: Polish source interviews; manuscript does not clearly state whether all model inputs remained Polish
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: highly sensitive mental-health narratives, anonymized before external-model analysis
evidence_records.Model family: OpenAI GPT; Google Gemini; Anthropic Claude
evidence_records.Exact model/version: GPT-4o; Gemini 2.5 Pro; Claude 4 Opus, described as August 2025 state of the art; default hyperparameters
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: investigator-persona simulation plus CO-STAR context/objective/style/tone/audience/response; prior meta-synthesis, textbook method, demographics and research questions; three analyses per model followed by synthesis
evidence_records.Fine-tuning or adaptation: none; in-context persona and domain/method conditioning
evidence_records.Agent roles: each model acts as a simulated primary investigator and thematic analyst; final within-model synthesis combines three iterations
evidence_records.Human role: two original-study experts map semantic/thematic overlap and verify novel themes; two independent external experts read raw data and blindly score all outputs; 115 public raters judge isolated themes
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: complete corpus for model analysis; themes/theme descriptions for expert, embedding and public evaluation
evidence_records.Generated outputs: themes and descriptions, within-model syntheses, overlap mappings, validity scores, embeddings and public authorship/content judgments
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: experts verify outputs directly against the full raw corpus and prompts are reproduced; models produce thematic syntheses rather than a fully auditable segment-to-code ledger
evidence_records.Baselines: published human phenomenological analysis of the same corpus; cross-model comparison; blinded expert and public judgments
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: three analysis rounds per model followed by one synthesis; UMAP random_state=42; default model sampling parameters
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: semantic-overlap percentage, Jaccard coefficient, Qwen3-Embedding-8B cosine similarity, StyleDistance cosine similarity and UMAP
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: two internal experts conduct non-blinded overlap/omission checks; two external experts blinded to source read all raw data and rate eight qualitative-validity dimensions; 115 Prolific raters judge shuffled isolated themes without raw data
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: two original clinical/phenomenology investigators; two external clinical/phenomenology experts; 115 nonexpert Prolific participants
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: Krippendorff alpha: human=.55, GPT=.69, Gemini=.84, Claude=.81 for four expert raters
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: Kruskal–Wallis tests with Dunn–Bonferroni post hoc comparisons, correlations/elasticity analyses, embedding cosine comparisons and UMAP
evidence_records.Principal results: Semantic overlap with the human interpretation was GPT 0%, Gemini 42% and Claude 58%; Jaccard was .21/.27/.28. Each model surfaced one author-verified omitted theme. External-expert mean validity was human 4.56, Gemini 4.21, Claude 3.68 and GPT 2.65; human and Gemini did not differ significantly. Public theme-title match favored Claude 4.17 and Gemini 4.06 over human 3.95/GPT 3.68, but public raters lacked raw data.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: no analysis time or API cost; authors infer fewer words may achieve near-human ratings, but this is not a workflow-efficiency study
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: reference protocol approved KB-367/23 with consent; transcripts anonymized; Prolific participants consented; closed models received clinical narratives, and authors recommend local open models for optimal deployment
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: verbatim prompting protocol and generated themes in appendices; named embedding models and UMAP settings; raw clinical data and execution code not reported as public
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: only two external experts; public raters lacked raw data and expertise; results depend on prompting; output stability varied; closed-model safety risks; models produced thematic constellations rather than integrated phenomenological structures
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: The abstract's claim that all models 'proved' capacity to mitigate human bias overstates one author-verified omitted theme per model. Verbosity correlated with expert scores, and three within-model runs are collapsed into a synthesis rather than reported as a stability distribution.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Direct reanalysis of the authors' prior human BPD phenomenology study; not an independent dataset or human benchmark.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Materially strengthens the case for raw-data-blinded specialist evaluation, multiple model families and verbosity controls; supports AI as a contrastive second reading, not proof of bias mitigation.

evidence_records.Full citation: Balt, Elias, Salim Salmi, Sandjai Bhulai, Stefan Vrinzen, Merijn Eikelenboom, Renske Gilissen, Daan Creemers, Arne Popma, and Saskia Mérelle. 2025. Deductively Coding Psychosocial Autopsy Interview Data Using a Few-Shot Learning Large Language Model. Frontiers in Public Health 13:1512537. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1512537.
evidence_records.Title: Deductively coding psychosocial autopsy interview data using a few-shot learning large language model
evidence_records.Authors: Elias Balt; Salim Salmi; Sandjai Bhulai; Stefan Vrinzen; Merijn Eikelenboom; Renske Gilissen; Daan Creemers; Arne Popma; Saskia Mérelle
evidence_records.Publication history notes: received 16 October 2024; accepted 29 January 2025; published 19 February 2025
evidence_records.Citation count, source, and retrieval da: not collected; publisher/PMC full text inspected 2026-08-24
evidence_records.Research objective: Evaluate whether a locally hosted few-shot LLM can deductively code and summarize sensitive psychosocial-autopsy interviews with sufficient agreement and usable source-grounded summaries.
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: Llama 3 70B classifies code applicability to segments, applies overlapping sliding windows to full transcripts, and summarizes positive windows for predefined codes; model labels are compared with researcher coding and two researchers qualitatively rate the summaries.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: deductive model coding with human review and proposed subsequent human inductive analysis
evidence_records.Dataset name: Dutch psychosocial autopsy study of railway suicides
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: restricted; potential access only under MREC criteria and reasonable request
evidence_records.Number of participants: bereaved respondents represented in 38 interviews; exact number of unique respondents not separately reported in the inspected text
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: 2,666 researcher-coded fragments; 1,254 LLM summaries qualitatively assessed; up to 30,000 words per interview
evidence_records.Document length: full interviews up to 30,000 words; model windows up to 300 words with overlap 75
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: highly sensitive and potentially identifying suicide-bereavement interviews
evidence_records.Exact model/version: Meta-Llama-3-70B-Instruct, locally hosted via Hugging Face; 8,192-token context
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: few-shot binary classification and code-focused summarization; preliminary synthetic-data work and one transcript used for prompt engineering; one positive and one negative example per code removed from evaluation
evidence_records.Fine-tuning or adaptation: no weight training; few-shot in-context examples
evidence_records.Agent roles: binary code classifier, sliding-window labeler and source-referenced summarizer
evidence_records.Human role: researchers create and consensus-resolve the reference coding, engineer prompts/examples, and independently rate summaries before discussion
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: coded fragment for binary classification; overlapping 300-word transcript window for full-corpus application; code-specific summary
evidence_records.Generated outputs: binary code labels, code frequencies and source-referenced summaries
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: summaries point back to original data/code locations, enabling human verification; restricted source data limit external audit
evidence_records.Baselines: manual coding by two independent researchers with third-researcher consensus
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: one main model run per task; no repeat seeds reported
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, Cohen's kappa and code-frequency ratios
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: two researchers independently rate each summary good/adequate/poor and analyze error themes, then resolve interpretations
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: two qualitative researchers plus a third consensus researcher for the manual corpus; two researchers for summary-quality review
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: binary model–researcher Cohen's kappa=.68; no reliability coefficient reported for good/adequate/poor summary ratings
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: descriptive accuracy, sensitivity/specificity, kappa, frequency ratios and qualitative error analysis
evidence_records.Principal results: Binary classification accuracy=.84 (SD=.09), kappa=.68; sliding-window transcript classification accuracy=.67. About 80% of summaries were good/adequate, but 19.7% contained unsolicited elaboration, 3.0% omitted crucial information and 1.3% hallucinated.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: model took about 5 hours per interview versus about 4 human coding hours, but processed all 38 over 8 days versus a four-month human project calendar; proposed speedups were not tested
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: MREC Amsterdam UMC NL76295.029.21; written consent; sensitive data restricted; model run locally
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: publisher supplementary material and exact open model identifier; data restricted; executable code and complete prompts not clearly deposited
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: corpus too small for training/test examples; 8,192-token context required windows that disrupted chronology; Dutch-only dataset; post-coding interpretation/time outside scope
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: The same research context shapes reference coding and output review; summary-rating reliability is absent. Calendar-time comparison is not equivalent to labor time, and the unoptimized model was slower per interview than a human.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Applies established psychosocial-autopsy manual coding and a prior corpus; no publication duplicate identified.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: A high-value benchmark for sensitive local deployment, source references and structured error audits; shows that good aggregate accuracy can coexist with chronology failures and clinically consequential hallucinations.

evidence_records.Full citation: Gao, Jie, Zhiyao Shu, Shun Yi Yeo, Alok Prakash, Chien-Ming Huang, Mark Dredze, and Ziang Xiao. 2025. Efficiency with Rigor! A Trustworthy LLM-powered Workflow for Qualitative Data Analysis. arXiv:2501.00775v3.
evidence_records.Title: Efficiency with Rigor! A Trustworthy LLM-powered Workflow for Qualitative Data Analysis
evidence_records.Authors: Jie Gao; Zhiyao Shu; Shun Yi Yeo; Alok Prakash; Chien-Ming Huang; Mark Dredze; Ziang Xiao
evidence_records.Peer-reviewed status: not peer reviewed / venue not verified
evidence_records.Publication history notes: arXiv v3 dated 26 October 2025; ACM template still contains placeholder conference acronym, 2018 date and XXXXX DOI, so it must not be represented as an accepted archival paper
evidence_records.Citation count, source, and retrieval da: not collected; official arXiv full text inspected 2026-08-24
evidence_records.Research objective: Design and evaluate a workflow that automates descriptive QDA stages while exposing reasoning and supporting analyst intervention, reflection and auditable codebooks.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: human-centered, trustworthy thematic analysis / qualitative data analysis
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: A GPT-5 web application chains raw text to open codes, subthemes, themes, findings and a theme map, with self-critique and user editing. Eight formative interviews derive requirements; a 12-person Latin-square comparison against Atlas.ti AI Coding and a blinded two-expert review assess experience/output quality; a separate six-dataset technical test uses lexical Jaccard coverage.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: primarily inductive; one participant demonstrates deductive use through research questions/predefined themes
evidence_records.Domain: HCI and general qualitative research tooling
evidence_records.Dataset name: six technical-evaluation text sets plus two public interview datasets on software quality and qualitative-data teaching
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: technical and study datasets described as supplementary/public; participant-study recordings not public
evidence_records.Number of documents: 72 technical-evaluation documents (12 each across six types); four roughly 1,000-word interview excerpts used across two user-study tasks
evidence_records.Number of participants: 8 formative QDA practitioners; 12 user-study analysts; 2 external evaluators
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: technical documents 2,000–4,000 words each; each user-study dataset consisted of two approximately 1,000-word interviews
evidence_records.Document length: 2,000–4,000 words in technical test; about 2,000 words per user-study dataset
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: public/non-sensitive task datasets; human-study recordings collected with consent
evidence_records.Exact model/version: GPT-5 via API with reasoning effort set to minimal; Atlas.ti baseline uses an undisclosed OpenAI model
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: four-stage prompt chain with about 1,000 instruction words per stage; user-defined code counts and prompts; self-critique, verification and JSON-constrained outputs; full prompt about 6,000 words in appendix/supplement
evidence_records.Agent roles: mechanical open coding, clustering, theme naming, quote preservation, self-critique, findings summary and DOT theme-map generation
evidence_records.Human role: analysts choose scope/specificity, inspect raw text and rationales, edit/regenerate codes and themes, prompt, memo and retain interpretive responsibility; authors/thematic analysts study use; external evaluators score outputs
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: text chunk, code, subtheme, theme and analyst interaction trajectory
evidence_records.Generated outputs: open codes tied to exact chunks, subthemes, themes, self-critiques, rationales, key findings, theme maps, memos, prompt history and final codebook trajectory
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: exact original chunks are retained under codes; users can reopen source text; prompts, changes, memos and trajectories are exported
evidence_records.Baselines: Atlas.ti AI Coding in a counterbalanced within-subject comparison
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: technical reasoning chain repeated five times per dataset; user tasks one run per participant/tool; seeds not reported
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: word-set Jaccard coverage from text to codes
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: 12 analysts use both systems on different datasets and complete Likert/think-aloud/interviews; two source-blinded external evaluators independently rate 24 codebooks on six questions spanning Lincoln–Guba trustworthiness dimensions
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: 12 analysts (4 expert, 6 intermediate, 2 novice self-reports); external E1 psychology PhD student with 4 years QDA, E2 data-science undergraduate with about 2 years QDA
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: not reported for external evaluators; user-interview analysis used first-author coding, second-author review/consensus and team member checking
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: paired t tests for external 10-point ratings; user Likert t tests were nonsignificant and reported descriptively
evidence_records.Principal results: Technical text-to-code lexical Jaccard averaged 89.6% (meeting transcripts 66.3%). User Likert differences were nonsignificant; MindCoder had higher descriptive agreement for flexibility/reflexivity/modification/ transparency, but Atlas.ti for efficiency and source engagement. Two experts rated MindCoder higher on all six questions (paired t, all p<.01), while noting redundancy, over-conceptualization and hierarchy errors.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: Atlas.ti was perceived faster (9 versus 7 agreeing); GPT-5 latency hindered some users; generation took about 15 minutes for more than 10,000 words and no cost accounting was reported
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: institutional IRB approval reported for formative and user studies; participant consent/recording described; model-provider data handling and exact protocol identifiers not reported
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: full prompts and technical dataset described in appendix/supplement plus Atlas.ti demo link; no verified public source-code repository or fixed model snapshot
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: eight formative participants mainly positivist; 12-person study; only Atlas.ti baseline and both use OpenAI models; expert evaluation preliminary; GPT-5 latency; other trustworthiness/triangulation strategies untested
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: Word-overlap Jaccard is incorrectly treated as content stability/trustworthiness and evaluates only text-to-code, not interpretive stages. External evaluation has only two raters with no reliability statistic, including one undergraduate; user-study output differences confound workflow, UI, model and verbosity.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Builds on prior LLM/QDA systems but no duplicate publication identified.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Adds a strong provenance/trajectory interface concept and highlights user-controlled iteration; ARR evaluation should replace lexical coverage with semantic/source-faithfulness audits and use more independent qualified raters.

evidence_records.Authors: Kentaro Hara; Reika Tachibana; Ryosuke Kumashiro; Kodai Ichihara; Takahiro Uemura; Hiroshi Maeda; Michiko Yamaguchi; Takahiro Inoue

evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: inductive thematic coding plus prompted scalar sentiment/subjectivity classification

evidence_records.Public or restricted data: available from corresponding author on reasonable request

evidence_records.Language: Japanese interview setting; transcript/model input language not explicitly reported
evidence_records.Exact model/version: ChatGPT-4o; snapshot, interface/API and date not reported
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: prompts and scoring instructions not reproduced in the article; the model codes themes and assigns emotion/subjectivity values

evidence_records.Generated outputs: codes, themes, emotional and subjectivity scores, co-occurrence network and clusters

evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: not reported; discrepancies resolved by discussion
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: descriptive score distributions and unspecific cluster analysis; algorithms/validation not sufficiently reported

evidence_records.Full citation: Mehta, Supriya D., Souvik Paul, Enid Awiti, Sophie Young, Garazi Zulaika, Fredrick O. Otieno, Penelope A. Phillips-Howard, Linda Mason, and Runa Bhaumik. 2025. evidence_records.Title: Evaluation of large language models within GenAI in qualitative research
evidence_records.Authors: Supriya D Mehta; Souvik Paul; Enid Awiti; Sophie Young; Garazi Zulaika; Fredrick O Otieno; Penelope A Phillips-Howard; Linda Mason; Runa Bhaumik
evidence_records.Publication history notes: received 13 February 2025; accepted 4 September 2025; published 7 October 2025
evidence_records.Citation count, source, and retrieval da: not collected; publisher/PMC full text inspected 2026-08-24
evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: CaCHe/CCG Kenyan FGD human analysis plus GPT-4o reanalysis
evidence_records.Research objective: Compare GPT-4o thematic and sentiment analysis with a rigorous prior human analysis, especially theme description, quote selection, quote support and hallucination.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: inductive thematic analysis and exploratory sentiment analysis
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: GPT-4o receives all translated FGD transcripts for girls and men separately, repeatedly generates subthemes until no new ones appear, then produces theme overviews and three supporting quotes; two original human analysts independently score outputs with a literature-derived rubric, and a separate prompted sentiment analysis is similarly reviewed.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: hybrid: initial themes generated inductively, then two human primary themes/subthemes are supplied in a later prompt; sentiment uses predefined categories
evidence_records.Domain: global public health / adolescent sexual and reproductive health
evidence_records.Dataset name: Cups and Community Health qualitative study nested in Cups or Cash for Girls trial
evidence_records.Number of documents: 11 FGD transcripts: 6 girl groups and 5 community-men groups
evidence_records.Number of participants: 54 adolescent girls/young women and 53 community men
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: 41,280 words for girls and 59,985 words for men; 13 girl themes and 11 male themes per evaluated result set
evidence_records.Language: English, Swahili and Dholuo collection; translated English supplied to model
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: sensitive sexual/reproductive-health discussions; consent and multiple IRBs
evidence_records.Exact model/version: reported as GPT-4o 'November 2023 version'; this label is internally suspect because GPT-4o did not exist in November 2023
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: standardized three-part prompt with questions, inductive theme request, later supplied primary themes/subthemes and exact-quote instructions; temperature tested .7–1.2 and fixed .7; max output 4,000 tokens
evidence_records.Agent roles: theme generator, quote selector, sentiment classifier and self-identified-bias reporter
evidence_records.Human role: two prior human analysts independently coded original data; the same two independently score model themes/quotes and resolve contextual interpretation; broader team resolves original disagreements
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: complete sex-specific transcript corpus for themes; selected quotation for evaluation
evidence_records.Generated outputs: themes/subthemes, overviews, keywords, supporting quotes, sentiment categories/quotes and bias inventory
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: model is explicitly asked for exact quotes; two source-familiar evaluators trace quotes to transcripts and document alterations/hallucinations
evidence_records.Baselines: published independent human thematic analysis of the same data; repeat model result sets; VADER/circumplex sentiment category frameworks
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: thematic analysis repeated until no new themes; three evaluated result sets shown for each corpus; random seeds not reported
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: BERTScore F1 for subtheme repeat similarity (.89–.99), percent quote support, Cohen's kappa, Gwet's AC1 and percent rater agreement
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: two original analysts independently apply a COREQ/SRQR/CASP-informed rubric to theme explanation and each supporting quote; ratings reported separately with reliability statistics
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: two investigators who had independently conducted the original human qualitative analysis
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: percent agreement, Cohen's kappa and Gwet's AC1 reported by task/corpus; variable from fair to excellent and generally lower for male/sentiment judgments
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: descriptive proportions plus multiple inter-rater statistics; no inferential human–AI equivalence test
evidence_records.Principal results: Theme descriptions were almost always judged complete and no generated subtheme was rejected outright, but quote quality was poor: consistency 64–87% for girls and 33–79% for men; strong support 36–67% and 18–55%, respectively. Quote hallucinations changed words, truncated or combined text and sometimes reversed who was under pressure.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: no time or API cost comparison; authors note human checking/feedback may erase practical benefit
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: Maseno MUERC MSU/DRPI/MUERC/01021/21, UIC 2022-0220 and LSTM 21-087 approvals; written consent; translated sensitive data sent through an API/Colab workflow; the paper's assurance about OpenAI data access is broader than demonstrated
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: complete annotated code in supplement; prompts and repeat outputs in supplementary tables; dataset DOI 10.25417/uic.26495884.v1
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: secondary dataset not designed for AI evaluation; one setting/topic/method; variable rubric reliability; cultural/linguistic context mismatch; sentiment-category limitations
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: The reported model version/date is internally impossible or mislabeled. BERTScore stability of subtheme text does not establish thematic validity, and evaluators are source experts but not independent of the original benchmark.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Direct computational reanalysis of the authors' previously published human CaCHe qualitative study; not an independent dataset.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Materially raises quote-level provenance and culturally/linguistically stratified evaluation in ARR priority; stable themes cannot compensate for source-altering quotations.

evidence_records.Full citation: Shah, Syed Tauhid Ullah, Mohamad Hussein, Ann Barcomb, and Mohammad Moshirpour. 2025. From Inductive to Deductive: LLMs-Based Qualitative Data Analysis in Requirements Engineering. arXiv:2504.19384v1.

evidence_records.Authors: Syed Tauhid Ullah Shah; Mohamad Hussein; Ann Barcomb; Mohammad Moshirpour
evidence_records.Citation count, source, and retrieval da: not collected; official arXiv full text inspected 2026-08-24
evidence_records.Research objective: Compare Llama 2, Mistral and GPT-4 against human requirement labels across shot count, prompt length and contextual detail.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: inductive and deductive qualitative data analysis for requirements engineering
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: Two analysts assign one-word functional labels to requirement statements and reconcile a fixed ground truth; three LLMs then perform multiclass single-label classification under zero-, one- and few-shot prompts. evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: claimed inductive/deductive; operationalized as zero-/few-shot fixed-ground-truth classification
evidence_records.Dataset name: Library Management System and Smart Home System requirements from PURE plus unspecified web SRS/FRS documents
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: repository reported; precise analyzed sample not described in the paper
evidence_records.Number of participants: not applicable; requirements documents, not participant qualitative data
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: number of requirements, documents, classes and train/test instances not reported
evidence_records.Exact model/version: GPT-4 Turbo API; Mistral 7B and LLaMA-2 7B via Hugging Face; exact model repository revisions not reported
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: zero-, one- and three-example few-shot prompts; short/medium/long instruction variants; no/some/full system context; temperature 0
evidence_records.Human role: two software-requirements analysts independently label, calculate kappa and reconcile ground truth; authors design prompts and evaluate
evidence_records.Generated outputs: one-word functional/category labels mapped to requirements
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: labels remain linked to requirement statements and repository is cited; no theme/code hierarchy or interpretive memo
evidence_records.Baselines: two-human consensus ground truth and three-model comparison across prompt conditions
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: multiple runs claimed for SD/ICC, but number of runs and seeds not reported
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: Cohen's kappa, accuracy, precision, recall, F1, standard deviation and intraclass correlation coefficient
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: no independent qualitative evaluation beyond the two analysts who created the reference labels
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: two software-engineering analysts with 1.5 years and 8 months requirements experience
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: human–human kappa .80 Library/.78 Smart Home; best GPT–human kappa .738/.734
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: descriptive metric tables; ICC formulation, confidence intervals and significance testing not reported
evidence_records.Principal results: GPT-4 few-shot kappa=.738/.734 and accuracy=.86/.85, versus zero-shot kappa=.543/.541 and accuracy=.72/.71. Long/full-context prompts performed best. GPT consistency is reported as ICC .93/.92, but repeat count is absent.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: human coding reported as 74 total hours; LLM manual-effort reduction asserted without model runtime or cost
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: no ethics statement; public requirements appear non-sensitive
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: GitHub repository https://github.com/SyedTauhidUllahShah/LLM4QDARE; prompt templates in paper; exact analyzed N, run count and model revisions absent
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: two test systems may not represent diverse real systems; dataset/documents and prompts may not cover specialized contexts; model and human bias
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: The 'inductive' condition is not inductive thematic analysis: it is one-label classification evaluated against a pre-existing consensus label set. evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: extends QDAcity-RE/autocoding and requirements-classification work; no duplicate publication identified
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: A key claimed-versus-operationalized counterexample for RQ2; useful for prompt ablation, but should not support claims about inductive theme discovery.

evidence_records.Title: Generative AI for thematic analysis in a maternal health study: coding semistructured interviews using large language models
evidence_records.Authors: Shan Qiao; Xingyu Fang; Junbo Wang; Ran Zhang; Xiaoming Li; Yuhao Kang
evidence_records.Publication history notes: published online 16 May 2025; version of record supersedes medRxiv v2 DOI 10.1101/2024.09.16.24313707
evidence_records.Citation count, source, and retrieval da: not collected; publisher/PMC version of record inspected 2026-08-24
evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: Qiao et al. maternal-health journal/preprint publication family
evidence_records.Research objective: Develop and evaluate a ChatGPT pipeline for question-filtered inductive coding of maternal-health provider interviews, comparing generated codes and time with a prior manual analysis.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: postpositivist inductive coding within Braun and Clarke thematic analysis
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: Nine transcripts are converted to question–answer rows; ChatGPT 4 filters dialogues by 20 interview questions, generates about 10 codes per question and aggregates similar codes. Two human coders review whether each AI code is accepted and BERT cosine similarity compares AI/human code text; workflow time is estimated.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: hybrid: codes are generated without a supplied codebook but are constrained and partitioned by a predetermined 20-question interview guide
evidence_records.Dataset name: South Carolina maternity-care provider interviews from a prior racial-disparities study
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: transcripts not public; source protocol cited
evidence_records.Number of participants: 9 maternity-care providers; 39 mothers existed in the source study but their transcripts were explicitly excluded from this AI analysis
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: 20 interview-guide questions; about 10 generated codes per question; exact words/dialogues not reported
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: health-provider interviews; deidentified; mothers from ethnic-minority groups excluded from AI processing because of ethical/privacy concerns
evidence_records.Exact model/version: reported only as ChatGPT 4 via web interface during prompt development and then API; snapshot/date and inference parameters not reported
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: structured question-by-question dialogue filtering, code generation and code aggregation; prompts shown in figures; repeated prompts used for an informal stability check
evidence_records.Agent roles: question/dialogue filter, inductive code generator and semantic code aggregator
evidence_records.Human role: two assistants had cleaned transcripts; two human coders provide prior codes and review/accept AI-generated codes; domain experts remain responsible for review and interpretation
evidence_records.Generated outputs: dialogue IDs, fine-grained codes and aggregated higher-level code categories
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: dialogue IDs preserve links from filtered responses to transcript rows; acceptance counts audit generated codes, but public source-level reproduction is unavailable
evidence_records.Baselines: prior manual coding by two human coders
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: same questions prompted multiple times for stability; number of repetitions and seeds not reported
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: human-accepted code percentage and BERT cosine similarity among runs and between AI/human codes
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: two human coders judge whether generated codes are accepted; independence/blinding and disagreement handling are not fully reported
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: two human coders; domain expertise and independence details not reported
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: descriptive accuracy/acceptance percentages, cosine similarity and estimated workflow times
evidence_records.Principal results: 85.15% of generated codes were accepted across questions (range 66.67–100%); human–AI semantic similarity=.795 (maximum .879); repeated AI code sets reportedly exceeded .95 similarity. AI codes were often more general and less domain-specific.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: manual workflow estimated 30.5 hours; AI setup about 5 hours plus 20 minutes generation, presented as 81% less time, but downstream expert-review time was not measured
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: University of South Carolina amendment Pro00115169 approved transcript reuse; data deidentified; mothers from ethnic-minority groups excluded from AI use; privacy risks explicitly discussed
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: workflow/prompt figures in full text; source study cited; no public transcripts, executable code, exact model snapshot or complete output package reported
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: single specific interview corpus; one unspecified ChatGPT model; no domain training; anchoring bias in human acceptance judgments; best validation practices unresolved
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: The 'accuracy' denominator is author acceptance of AI-proposed codes, not independent recovery of a fixed or plural human target; evaluators may be anchored by AI output. evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Version of record for medRxiv DOI 10.1101/2024.09.16.24313707; uses provider subset from Zhang et al.'s prior human study. Merge only the journal version.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Supports question-conditioned pipelines and explicit time accounting, but ARR should use independent/blinded code review, include all review labor and retain participant groups rather than excluding them from AI evaluation.

quality_scores.Title: Codebook Reduction and Saturation: Novel observations on Inductive Thematic Saturation for Large Language Models and initial coding in Thematic Analysis

Clarity of its qualitative methodology.rationale: Initial-coding, reduction and ITS steps are described in detail, while ITS is not equivalent to thematic validity.

Appropriateness of its dataset.rationale: Twelve real interviews support the stability question, though one corpus limits transferability.

Transparency of its computational workfl.rationale: Model, temperature, prompts, DSPy construction and training-pair counts are reported.

Strength and independence of its baselin.rationale: Prompt_2 is a useful procedural baseline but there is no human or gold duplicate baseline.

Adequacy of its human evaluation.rationale: No independent human evaluation of code or reduction quality.

Validity of its automatic metrics.rationale: CoV and similarity characterize stability, but the unvalidated ITS ratio cannot establish validity.

Treatment of interpretive plurality.rationale: Alternative interpretations and legitimate codebook plurality are collapsed into duplicates.

Evidence grounding and traceability.rationale: Representative quotes accompany initial codes, but reduced-code source mapping is incompletely audited.

Stability and reproducibility testing.rationale: Seven repeats plus six sequences directly test variability.

Ethics, privacy, and responsible-researc.rationale: No study-specific ethics/privacy reporting for the secondary corpus.

Availability of data, prompts, code, and.rationale: Prompts and source DOI are available; code and complete outputs are not.

Whether conclusions are proportionate to.rationale: Authors acknowledge complexity/cost, but their claim of precise/valid ITS exceeds evidence without human semantic validation.

quality_scores.Interpretation caution: Audit aid only; totals are not study rankings and every dimension must be read with its evidence.

quality_scores.Title: Comparing a Human’s and a Multi-Agent System’s Thematic Analysis: Assessing Qualitative Coding Consistency

Clarity of its qualitative methodology.rationale: Braun–Clarke iTA and the code/theme evaluation framework are explicit.

Appropriateness of its dataset.rationale: 184 domain-specific responses make a relevant benchmark, but respondent/response accounting is incomplete.

Transparency of its computational workfl.rationale: Agent roles and process prompt are described; exact snapshot, parameters and code are absent.

Strength and independence of its baselin.rationale: A prior four-expert analysis of the identical corpus is a strong comparator but not independent of the study family.

Adequacy of its human evaluation.rationale: Two blinded external domain experts review both code- and theme-level outputs.

Validity of its automatic metrics.rationale: Descriptive ratings and binomial tests are useful, but no equivalence design or external-rater reliability is supplied.

Treatment of interpretive plurality.rationale: Evaluator divergence is visible but largely summarized rather than modeled as legitimate plurality.

Evidence grounding and traceability.rationale: Responses are paired to code sets and themes to codes; final narrative provenance remains weaker.

Stability and reproducibility testing.rationale: Only one MAS run is reported.

Ethics, privacy, and responsible-researc.rationale: Anonymous reuse consent is reported; provider/privacy controls are not.

Availability of data, prompts, code, and.rationale: OSF data and process prompt plus published/preprint DOIs are available, but no full system/run package.

Whether conclusions are proportionate to.rationale: Hybrid conclusion is cautious, yet claims of approaching human depth/coherence overread two discordant evaluators and one corpus.

quality_scores.Interpretation caution: Audit aid only; totals are not study rankings and every dimension must be read with its evidence.

quality_scores.Title: Computational Phenomenology of Borderline Personality Disorder: A Comparative Evaluation of LLM-Simulated Expert Personas and Human Clinical Experts

Clarity of its qualitative methodology.rationale: Phenomenological goals, persona conditioning and evaluation stages are unusually explicit.

Appropriateness of its dataset.rationale: A long, difficult clinical corpus directly tests latent interpretation, albeit only one homogeneous setting.

Transparency of its computational workfl.rationale: Named models, default settings, full staged prompts and embedding settings are reported.

Strength and independence of its baselin.rationale: Published human analysis, three models, internal/external experts and public raters provide layered baselines.

Adequacy of its human evaluation.rationale: Two raw-data-reading blinded specialists plus internal and public assessments offer depth and breadth.

Validity of its automatic metrics.rationale: Overlap, reliability, nonparametric tests and embeddings are appropriate when read as complementary measures.

Treatment of interpretive plurality.rationale: Four expert scores expose disagreement, but the design still averages plural judgments and treats human themes as a reference.

Evidence grounding and traceability.rationale: External experts read the entire source corpus and prompts/outputs are appendixed, though no segment ledger exists.

Stability and reproducibility testing.rationale: Three runs per model are synthesized rather than reported as a stability distribution.

Ethics, privacy, and responsible-researc.rationale: Approval, consent, anonymization and closed-model risk/local-model recommendation are explicit.

Availability of data, prompts, code, and.rationale: Prompts/outputs and model names are available, but raw clinical data, code and fixed snapshots are not.

Whether conclusions are proportionate to.rationale: Limitations are strong, but abstract language that omitted themes 'prove' bias mitigation is disproportionate.

quality_scores.Interpretation caution: Audit aid only; totals are not study rankings and every dimension must be read with its evidence.

quality_scores.Title: Deductively coding psychosocial autopsy interview data using a few-shot learning large language model

Clarity of its qualitative methodology.rationale: Deductive classification, windowing, summarization and researcher roles are clear.

Appropriateness of its dataset.rationale: Thirty-eight long, sensitive interviews are a substantively demanding corpus.

Transparency of its computational workfl.rationale: Open-model identifier, local hosting, windows and few-shot construction are well reported.

Strength and independence of its baselin.rationale: Independent researcher coding with consensus supplies a credible baseline.

Adequacy of its human evaluation.rationale: Two researchers rate 1,254 summaries, but rating reliability/blinding are not reported.

Validity of its automatic metrics.rationale: Accuracy, sensitivity/specificity and kappa are well matched to deductive labels and paired with error analysis.

Treatment of interpretive plurality.rationale: Consensus coding and error review are present, but alternative valid coding is not explicitly preserved.

Evidence grounding and traceability.rationale: Summaries reference source data and errors are audited at the fragment level.

Stability and reproducibility testing.rationale: No repeat-run stability test or seed report.

Ethics, privacy, and responsible-researc.rationale: Formal approval, consent, restriction and local deployment are exemplary.

Availability of data, prompts, code, and.rationale: Supplement and model are available; data are restricted and code/prompts not fully deposited.

Whether conclusions are proportionate to.rationale: Conclusions retain human responsibility and distinguish coding from interpretation/time, proportionate to observed failures.

quality_scores.Interpretation caution: Audit aid only; totals are not study rankings and every dimension must be read with its evidence.

quality_scores.Title: Efficiency with Rigor! A Trustworthy LLM-powered Workflow for Qualitative Data Analysis

Clarity of its qualitative methodology.rationale: Human/LLM task allocation and staged QDA workflow are explicit.

Appropriateness of its dataset.rationale: Multiple text types and two interview datasets support interface evaluation, though user tasks are short/simplified.

Transparency of its computational workfl.rationale: GPT-5, reasoning setting, prompt chain, schemas and appendixed prompts are reported.

Strength and independence of its baselin.rationale: Atlas.ti is relevant but confounds model, UI and workflow and discloses no model version.

Adequacy of its human evaluation.rationale: User and blinded output studies are useful, but only two external raters include one undergraduate and lack reliability.

Validity of its automatic metrics.rationale: Lexical Jaccard measures word retention, not qualitative faithfulness or downstream thematic validity.

Treatment of interpretive plurality.rationale: Memos and analyst editing support reflection, but automated self-critique and averaged ratings do not preserve plural interpretations.

Evidence grounding and traceability.rationale: Source chunks, rationales, prompt history, edits and trajectory provide strong auditability.

Stability and reproducibility testing.rationale: Five technical repetitions are reported, though user-output stability is not.

Ethics, privacy, and responsible-researc.rationale: IRB and consent are reported; provider data handling/protocol identifiers are thin.

Availability of data, prompts, code, and.rationale: Prompts/datasets are supplemental; no verified code repository or fixed snapshot.

Whether conclusions are proportionate to.rationale: Authors note major constraints, but claims that lexical retention makes the reasoning chain reliable/trustworthy overstate the metric.

quality_scores.Interpretation caution: Audit aid only; totals are not study rankings and every dimension must be read with its evidence.

quality_scores.Title: Emotional analysis of operating room nurses in acute care hospitals in Japan: insights using ChatGPT

Appropriateness of its dataset.rationale: Ten short single-center interviews suit exploration but not claimed general benefits.

Transparency of its computational workfl.rationale: Model snapshot, access mode, prompts, parameters and output logs are absent.

Strength and independence of its baselin.rationale: Two human researchers provide a comparator, but its item-level structure is not reported.

Validity of its automatic metrics.rationale: Unvalidated -100/+100 scales and unspecified clustering cannot establish objective emotion/subjectivity measurement.

quality_scores.Title: Evaluation of large language models within GenAI in qualitative research

Clarity of its qualitative methodology.rationale: Human and AI thematic procedures and the confirmability-focused rubric are explicit.

Appropriateness of its dataset.rationale: Eleven long multilingual/culturally specific FGDs form a demanding and relevant corpus.

Transparency of its computational workfl.rationale: API workflow, prompts, temperature tests and token cap are reported, despite an impossible model/date label.

Strength and independence of its baselin.rationale: A rigorous prior two-analyst thematic analysis of the same data anchors comparison.

Adequacy of its human evaluation.rationale: No independent qualitative judgment beyond the two ground-truth annotators.

Validity of its automatic metrics.rationale: Classification metrics fit the operational task, but ICC/repeat design lacks essential details.

Treatment of interpretive plurality.rationale: One consensus ground truth erases alternative labels and no interpretive plurality is examined.

Evidence grounding and traceability.rationale: Labels link to statements, but no qualitative code/theme provenance or audit trail is evaluated.

Stability and reproducibility testing.rationale: SD/ICC imply repeats, yet run number and seeds are absent.

Ethics, privacy, and responsible-researc.rationale: Non-sensitive public requirements make ethics low-risk, though no statement is supplied.

Availability of data, prompts, code, and.rationale: Repository and prompt templates exist, but exact N, run count and model revisions are absent.

Whether conclusions are proportionate to.rationale: Manual-effort, reliability and reduced-subjectivity claims are unsupported, and results cannot support inductive thematic discovery.

quality_scores.Title: Generative AI for thematic analysis in a maternal health study: coding semistructured interviews using large language models

Clarity of its qualitative methodology.rationale: Postpositivist stance and filtering/generation/aggregation steps are clear, though question conditioning narrows induction.

Appropriateness of its dataset.rationale: Nine real provider interviews support a case study; excluding mothers narrows transferability.

Transparency of its computational workfl.rationale: Prompts/workflow are shown but exact model snapshot and parameters are missing.

Strength and independence of its baselin.rationale: Prior human codes are a relevant baseline, but evaluator independence and reconciliation are unclear.

Adequacy of its human evaluation.rationale: Two human coders accept/reject AI codes, with no blinding, reliability or detailed expertise.

Validity of its automatic metrics.rationale: Acceptance percentage and cosine similarity are interpretable only as coarse code-overlap proxies.

Treatment of interpretive plurality.rationale: Two coders and postpositivist framing are acknowledged, but acceptance collapses disagreement and risks anchoring.

Evidence grounding and traceability.rationale: Dialogue IDs maintain source linkage through filtering and coding.

Stability and reproducibility testing.rationale: Repeated prompts yield >.95 similarity, but repetition count/seeds are missing.

Ethics, privacy, and responsible-researc.rationale: IRB amendment, deidentification, sensitive-group exclusion and privacy risks are explicitly considered.

Availability of data, prompts, code, and.rationale: Prompt figures and source study exist; transcripts, code, snapshot and full outputs are unavailable.

Whether conclusions are proportionate to.rationale: Limitations acknowledge anchoring, but 85.15% 'accuracy' and 81% time-saving language overstates nonindependent acceptance and omits review labor.
